claim: Cartilage specification requires Sox9, a transcription factor with broad roles for organogenesis outside the skeletal system.
source: The specification of cartilage requires Sox9, a transcription factor with broad roles for organogenesis outside the skeletal system.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the introduction's discussion of Sox9's roles in multiple organ systems.

claim: Cartilage-associated chromatin accessibility is dynamically established during neural crest cell differentiation into chondrocytes.
source: By analyzing chromatin accessibility during the differentiation of neural crest cells into chondrocytes of the zebrafish head, we find that cartilage-associated chromatin accessibility is dynamically established.
evidence: This is supported by µATACseq data showing progressive establishment of accessibility at different developmental stages (36, 48, and 72 hpf).

claim: Cartilage-associated regions that become accessible after neural crest migration are co-enriched for Sox9 and Fox transcription factor binding motifs.
source: Cartilage-associated regions that become accessible after neural crest migration are co-enriched for Sox9 and Fox transcription factor binding motifs.
evidence: This is supported by de novo motif analysis showing Sox and Fox motifs as top enriched motifs in chondrocyte-specific accessible regions.

claim: In zebrafish lacking Foxc1 paralogs, there is a global decrease in chromatin accessibility in chondrocytes.
source: In zebrafish lacking Foxc1 paralogs, we find a global decrease in chromatin accessibility in chondrocytes, consistent with a later loss of dorsal facial cartilages.
evidence: This is supported by µATACseq data comparing Foxc1 mutants to controls, showing reduced accessibility at many cartilage-associated elements.

claim: Many Foxc1-dependent elements function as enhancers with region- and stage-specific activity in facial cartilages.
source: Zebrafish transgenesis assays confirm that many of these Foxc1-dependent elements function as enhancers with region- and stage-specific activity in facial cartilages.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assays showing that 59% (13/22) of tested Foxc1-dependent elements drove GFP expression in facial chondrocytes.

claim: Foxc1 promotes chondrogenesis in the face by establishing chromatin accessibility at cartilage-associated gene enhancers.
source: These results show that Foxc1 promotes chondrogenesis in the face by establishing chromatin accessibility at a number of cartilage-associated gene enhancers.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the combination of accessibility data in mutants and enhancer validation experiments.

claim: Sox9 is essential for chondrogenic differentiation in all vertebrates examined.
source: The transcription factor Sox9 is essential for chondrogenic differentiation in all vertebrates examined (Bi et al., 1999; Lefebvre et al., 1997; Mori-Akiyama et al., 2003; Yan et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Sox9 has widespread roles outside the skeletal system, including the reproductive system, kidney, liver, and skin.
source: yet it also has widespread roles outside the skeletal system, including the reproductive system, kidney, liver, and skin (Jo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jo et al., 2014.

claim: Sox9 directly binds to cis-regulatory elements adjacent to chondrogenic genes including Col2a1, Col10a1, and Acan.
source: Sox9 is known to directly bind to a number of cis-regulatory elements adjacent to chondrogenic genes, including Col2a1, Col10a1, and Acan (Askary et al., 2015; Dy et al., 2012; Lefebvre et al., 1997; Ohba et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Sox9 is dispensable for chromatin accessibility at chondrogenic enhancers.
source: It is, however, dispensable for chromatin accessibility at these same elements (Liu et al., 2018), suggesting that other unknown factors may first open chromatin at chondrogenic enhancers for later activation by Sox9.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: HNF3/FoxA binds closed chromatin at enhancers and makes these more accessible in the endoderm lineage.
source: In the endoderm lineage, HNF3/FoxA binds closed chromatin at enhancers and makes these more accessible (Cirillo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cirillo et al., 2002.

claim: Foxd3 has been proposed to establish chromatin accessibility in the early neural crest lineage.
source: Foxd3 has been similarly proposed to establish chromatin accessibility in the early neural crest lineage (Lukoseviciute et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lukoseviciute et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of Foxc1 in mouse results in widespread cartilage and bone defects.
source: In mouse, loss of Foxc1 results in widespread cartilage and bone defects (Kume et al., 1998), including impaired tracheal and rib cartilages (Hong et al., 1999), loss of calvarial bone due to premature ossification (Rice et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2013; Vivatbutsiri et al., 2008), syngnathia (Inman et al., 2013), and disruption of endochondral bone maturation (Yoshida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous mouse studies.

claim: Loss of both Foxc1 paralogs in zebrafish results in severe reductions of dorsal cartilages of the upper face.
source: In zebrafish, loss of both Foxc1 paralogs (foxc1a and foxc1b) results in severe reductions of dorsal cartilages of the upper face, which are preceded by reduced expression of several Sox9 targets, including col2a1a, acana, matn1, and matn4 (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2018.

claim: Sox9 ChIP-Seq in dissected mouse rib and nose cartilage revealed enrichment of Fox binding motifs within Sox9-bound cis-regulatory sequences near chondrogenic genes.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by deep sequencing (ChIP-Seq) using a Sox9 antibody in dissected mouse rib and nose cartilage revealed enrichment of Fox binding motifs within Sox9-bound cis-regulatory sequences near chondrogenic genes (Ohba et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ohba et al., 2015.

claim: The analysis yielded 33,679 distal accessible elements, with 5736 elements over-enriched in chondrocytes and 8955 elements under-enriched in chondrocytes.
source: This analysis yielded 33,679 distal accessible elements, with 5736 elements over-enriched in chondrocytes and 8955 elements under-enriched in chondrocytes (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The cartilage-specific R2 enhancer of col2a1a is enriched in chondrocyte-specific elements.
source: As confirmation of sequence quality, the cartilage-specific R2 enhancer of the Collagen Type II alpha 1 a gene (col2a1a) is enriched in chondrocyte-specific elements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: De novo motif analysis of the top 2000 chondrocyte-enriched regions recovered motifs for Sox, Fox, Nfat, Zfx, and Nkx transcription factor families.
source: De novo motif analysis of the top 2000 chondrocyte-enriched regions using HOMER recovered motifs for Sox, Fox, Nfat, Zfx, and Nkx transcription factor families (Figure 1D; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Consensus sequences for Sox, Fox, and Nfat motifs were highly similar between zebrafish and mouse.
source: Consensus sequences for Sox, Fox, and Nfat motifs were highly similar between zebrafish and mouse (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of the nearest genes to the chondrocyte-enriched elements revealed cartilage development as one of the top six associated terms.
source: In addition, Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of the nearest genes to the chondrocyte-enriched elements revealed cartilage development as one of the top six associated terms (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CNCCs are first specified at ~10.5 hpf at the border of the neural keel.
source: CNCCs are first specified at ~10.5 hpf at the border of the neural keel, finish their migration into the pharyngeal arches by ~20 hpf, and then show the first histological signs of cartilage development in the jaw at ~52 hpf (Schilling and Kimmel, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schilling and Kimmel, 1997.

claim: CNCCs finish their migration into the pharyngeal arches by ~20 hpf.
source: CNCCs are first specified at ~10.5 hpf at the border of the neural keel, finish their migration into the pharyngeal arches by ~20 hpf, and then show the first histological signs of cartilage development in the jaw at ~52 hpf (Schilling and Kimmel, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schilling and Kimmel, 1997.

claim: CNCCs show the first histological signs of cartilage development in the jaw at ~52 hpf.
source: CNCCs are first specified at ~10.5 hpf at the border of the neural keel, finish their migration into the pharyngeal arches by ~20 hpf, and then show the first histological signs of cartilage development in the jaw at ~52 hpf (Schilling and Kimmel, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schilling and Kimmel, 1997.

claim: CNCC-derived arch ectomesenchyme cells can be uniquely identified by co-expression of fli1a:GFP and sox10:Dsred transgenes at 36 and 48 hpf.
source: CNCC-derived arch ectomesenchyme cells can be uniquely identified by co-expression of fli1a:GFP and sox10:Dsred transgenes at 36 and 48 hpf (Askary et al., 2017), stages just prior to cartilage differentiation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Askary et al., 2017 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 4915 of 14,623 elements gaining accessibility from 36 to 48 hpf were linked to GO terms including skeletal system development and cartilage development.
source: 4915 of 14,623 elements gaining accessibility from 36 to 48 hpf were linked to GO terms including skeletal system development and cartilage development, and were enriched for Sox and Fox transcription factor binding motifs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elements gaining accessibility from 36 to 48 hpf were enriched for Sox and Fox transcription factor binding motifs.
source: 4915 of 14,623 elements gaining accessibility from 36 to 48 hpf were linked to GO terms including skeletal system development and cartilage development, and were enriched for Sox and Fox transcription factor binding motifs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4323 elements with decreasing accessibility from 36 to 48 hpf were linked to GO terms related to cellular migration and enriched for motifs of neural crest-associated transcription factors.
source: 4323 elements with decreasing accessibility were linked to several GO terms related to cellular migration and enriched for motifs of neural crest-associated transcription factors (Nr2f, Lhx, Olig2, Hox, Ets), consistent with decommissioning of enhancers involved in earlier neural crest migration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Of the 5,736 elements enriched in chondrocytes at 72 hpf, only 6% (356) had peak accessibility at 36 hpf with no further increase in accessibility by 48 hpf.
source: Of the 5,736 elements enriched in chondrocytes at 72 hpf, only 6% (356) had peak accessibility at 36 hpf with no further increase in accessibility by 48 hpf ('Group I').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 48% (2741) of chondrocyte-enriched elements displayed increased accessibility between 36 and 48 hpf.
source: In contrast, 48% (2741) displayed increased accessibility between 36 and 48 hpf ('Group II'), and 46% (2639) between 48 and 72 hpf ('Group III').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 46% (2639) of chondrocyte-enriched elements displayed increased accessibility between 48 and 72 hpf.
source: In contrast, 48% (2741) displayed increased accessibility between 36 and 48 hpf ('Group II'), and 46% (2639) between 48 and 72 hpf ('Group III').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Group I elements are enriched for predicted binding sites for members of the Nfat, Fox, Lhx, Nr2f, Meis, and Pax families.
source: For Group I, de novo motif enrichment revealed predicted binding sites for members of the Nfat, Fox, Lhx, Nr2f, Meis, and Pax families, and significant GO terms included neural crest migration, cell migration in general, and dorsal/ventral pattern formation (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Group I elements have significant GO terms including neural crest migration, cell migration in general, and dorsal/ventral pattern formation.
source: For Group I, de novo motif enrichment revealed predicted binding sites for members of the Nfat, Fox, Lhx, Nr2f, Meis, and Pax families, and significant GO terms included neural crest migration, cell migration in general, and dorsal/ventral pattern formation (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Group II and Group III elements share common predicted transcription factor binding motifs, including Sox dimer, Fox, Nfat, and Ap1 motifs.
source: Group II and Group III elements share many common predicted transcription factor binding motifs, including Sox dimer, Fox, Nfat, and Ap1 motifs previously described for mouse cartilage (Figure 2E,G; Supplementary file 1B; Ohba et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2E and 2G.

claim: An Nkx motif was recovered only for Group II elements.
source: An Nkx motif was recovered only for Group II (p=10−58, 36% of targets)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: An Egr motif was enriched for Group II versus Group III elements.
source: an Egr motif was enriched for Group II (p=10−65, 55% of targets) versus Group III (p=10−20, 16% of targets)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2E and 2G.

claim: A Tead motif was enriched for Group III versus Group II elements.
source: and a Tead motif was enriched for Group III (p=10−63, 36% of targets) versus Group II (p=10−20, 3% of targets).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2E and 2G.

claim: The majority of chondrocyte-specific elements gain accessibility after pharyngeal arch formation.
source: We therefore conclude that the majority of chondrocyte-specific elements gain accessibility after pharyngeal arch formation and that transcription factor binding motifs change during cartilage differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal analysis of accessibility shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transcription factor binding motifs change during cartilage differentiation.
source: We therefore conclude that the majority of chondrocyte-specific elements gain accessibility after pharyngeal arch formation and that transcription factor binding motifs change during cartilage differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the different motif enrichments in Group I, II, and III elements.

claim: In situ hybridization for foxc1a and foxc1b at 36 hpf showed partial overlap with the pou3f3b>GFP line in the dorsal-intermediate regions of the first and second arches.
source: In situ hybridization for foxc1a and foxc1b at 36 hpf showed partial overlap with the pou3f3b>GFP line in the dorsal-intermediate regions of the first and second arches (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reductions of cartilage were observed in the pou3f3b>GFP domain of Foxc1 mutants at 6 dpf.
source: Consistently, we observed reductions of cartilage in the pou3f3b>GFP domain of mutants at 6 days post-fertilization (dpf), except in the dorsal-most regions (close to the ear) that are pou3f3b>GFP-positive yet foxc1a/foxc1b-negative (Figure 3C,D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 10% (120/1221) of Group I elements had reduced accessibility in Foxc1 mutants.
source: Analysis of cartilage-associated elements in Foxc1 mutants revealed that 10% (120/1221) of elements that have established peak accessibility by 36 hpf (i.e. Group I) and 41% (636/1556) of elements that increase accessibility between 36 and 48 hpf (i.e. Group II) had reduced accessibility in Foxc1 mutants (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: 41% (636/1556) of Group II elements had reduced accessibility in Foxc1 mutants.
source: Analysis of cartilage-associated elements in Foxc1 mutants revealed that 10% (120/1221) of elements that have established peak accessibility by 36 hpf (i.e. Group I) and 41% (636/1556) of elements that increase accessibility between 36 and 48 hpf (i.e. Group II) had reduced accessibility in Foxc1 mutants (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Foxa2 and Foxd3 motifs were enriched only in Foxc1-dependent Group I elements.
source: Whereas several types of Fox motifs were uncovered in both, a closer analysis revealed enrichment of Foxa2 and Foxd3 motifs only in Foxc1-dependent elements (p=10−45, 38% of targets; p=10−16, 18% of targets), and a Foxo1 motif only in Foxc1-independent elements (p=10−42, 49% of targets).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A Foxo1 motif was enriched only in Foxc1-independent Group I elements.
source: Whereas several types of Fox motifs were uncovered in both, a closer analysis revealed enrichment of Foxa2 and Foxd3 motifs only in Foxc1-dependent elements (p=10−45, 38% of targets; p=10−16, 18% of targets), and a Foxo1 motif only in Foxc1-independent elements (p=10−42, 49% of targets).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A Foxa1 motif was enriched only in Foxc1-dependent Group II elements.
source: Similarly in Group II elements, a Foxa1 motif was enriched only in Foxc1-dependent elements (p=10−59, 38% of targets), and Foxh1 and Foxp1 motifs only in Foxc1-independent elements (p=10−22, 22% of targets; p=10−19, 7% of targets) (Figure 3G, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Foxh1 and Foxp1 motifs were enriched only in Foxc1-independent Group II elements.
source: Similarly in Group II elements, a Foxa1 motif was enriched only in Foxc1-dependent elements (p=10−59, 38% of targets), and Foxh1 and Foxp1 motifs only in Foxc1-independent elements (p=10−22, 22% of targets; p=10−19, 7% of targets) (Figure 3G, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The consensus sequence for Foxc1-bound peaks is nearly identical to Foxa1/2 motifs.
source: Although Foxc1 motifs were not in the database used for motif predictions, the selective presence of Foxa1/2 motifs in Foxc1-dependent elements is consistent with previous reports that the consensus sequence for Foxc1-bound peaks is nearly identical to Foxa1/2 motifs (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: 33% (207/636) of Foxc1-dependent Group II elements had both Sox and Fox predicted motifs.
source: Whereas 33% (207/636) of Foxc1-dependent Group II elements had both Sox and Fox predicted motifs, only 16% (151/920) of Foxc1-independent Group II elements had both.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on motif analysis.

claim: Only 16% (151/920) of Foxc1-independent Group II elements had both Sox and Fox predicted motifs.
source: Whereas 33% (207/636) of Foxc1-dependent Group II elements had both Sox and Fox predicted motifs, only 16% (151/920) of Foxc1-independent Group II elements had both.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on motif analysis.

claim: 59% (13/22) of tested Foxc1-dependent Group II elements drove GFP expression in facial chondrocytes at 6 dpf.
source: We observed that 59% (13/22) of elements drove GFP expression in facial chondrocytes at 6 dpf.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by transgenic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: An element in the first intron of sox10 drove uniform cartilage-specific expression.
source: Whereas an element in the first intron of sox10 drove uniform cartilage-specific expression, most elements drove expression in specific sub-regions or particular differentiation stages of cartilage.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A distal 5′ element of ucmab drove expression in chondrocytes of multiple joints in the zebrafish head.
source: A distal 5′ element of ucmab drove expression in chondrocytes of multiple joints in the zebrafish head
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Three enhancer transgenes with diverse expression patterns (broad sox10, joint-restricted ucmab, and joint-excluded epyc enhancers) all displayed reduced activity specifically in the dorsal cartilage regions affected in Foxc1 mutants.
source: Furthermore, we found that three enhancer transgenes with diverse expression patterns (broad sox10, joint-restricted ucmab, and joint-excluded epyc enhancers) all displayed reduced activity specifically in the dorsal cartilage regions affected in Foxc1 mutants (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Four genes linked to Foxc1-dependent enhancers (sox10, lect1, col9a3, epyc) showed reduced expression in cartilage-forming regions of the dorsal arches of Foxc1 mutants.
source: We also confirmed by in situ hybridization that four genes linked to Foxc1-dependent enhancers (sox10, lect1, col9a3, epyc) showed reduced expression in cartilage-forming regions of the dorsal arches of Foxc1 mutants (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Foxc1 function is required for the accessibility of close to half of chondrocyte enhancers in the zebrafish face.
source: Our findings indicate that Foxc1 function is required for the accessibility of close to half of chondrocyte enhancers in the zebrafish face.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that 41% of Group II elements had reduced accessibility in Foxc1 mutants.

claim: Foxc1 likely has a similar function in chondrocyte enhancer accessibility throughout the body in mouse.
source: Given expression and function of Foxc1 in diverse cartilages (e.g. limb, rib, tracheal) in mouse, it seems likely that Foxc1 has a similar function in chondrocyte enhancer accessibility throughout the body.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known Foxc1 expression patterns in mouse.

claim: 33% of chondrocyte enhancers have co-enrichment of predicted Sox and Fox binding sites.
source: The co-enrichment of predicted Sox and Fox binding sites in 33% of chondrocyte enhancers suggests a model in which Foxc1 promotes Sox9 binding to these same enhancers by increasing chromatin accessibility, though this would require direct Sox9 binding studies to validate.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on motif analysis of Foxc1-dependent Group II elements.

claim: Foxc1 may promote Sox9 binding to enhancers by increasing chromatin accessibility.
source: The co-enrichment of predicted Sox and Fox binding sites in 33% of chondrocyte enhancers suggests a model in which Foxc1 promotes Sox9 binding to these same enhancers by increasing chromatin accessibility, though this would require direct Sox9 binding studies to validate.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the co-enrichment of Sox and Fox motifs in Foxc1-dependent elements.

claim: Not all Foxc1-dependent enhancers have predicted Fox binding motifs.
source: However, not all Foxc1-dependent enhancers have predicted Fox binding motifs, which might suggest indirect regulation of chromatin accessibility in at least some cases.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that only 33% of Foxc1-dependent Group II elements had both Sox and Fox motifs.

claim: Many enhancers do not appear to require Foxc1 activity.
source: In addition, many enhancers do not appear to require Foxc1 activity.
evidence: This is based on the finding that 59% of Group II elements were Foxc1-independent.

claim: Other members of the Fox family may compensate for Foxc1, such as Foxf1/2 in the facial midline.
source: It is possible that other members of the Fox family compensate, such as Foxf1/2 in the facial midline (Xu et al., 2018) and Foxa2/3 during later hypertrophic maturation (Ionescu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Foxa2/3 may compensate for Foxc1 during later hypertrophic maturation.
source: It is possible that other members of the Fox family compensate, such as Foxf1/2 in the facial midline (Xu et al., 2018) and Foxa2/3 during later hypertrophic maturation (Ionescu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Ionescu et al., 2012.

claim: There may be other co-factors that mediate chondrocyte enhancer accessibility and activation, such as Nkx3.2.
source: Alternatively, there may be other co-factors that mediate chondrocyte enhancer accessibility and activation, such as Nkx3.2.
evidence: This is speculation based on the enrichment of Nkx motifs in Foxc1-independent elements.

claim: Foxc1 lacks a chromatin modifying domain.
source: Foxc1 lacks a chromatin modifying domain (Yoshida et al., 2015) and therefore would need to interact with a co-factor to directly open chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2015.

claim: Foxc1 would need to interact with a co-factor to directly open chromatin.
source: Foxc1 lacks a chromatin modifying domain (Yoshida et al., 2015) and therefore would need to interact with a co-factor to directly open chromatin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of chromatin modifying domain in Foxc1.

claim: Foxc1 could act to maintain open chromatin, as shown for Foxa1 in the liver.
source: Foxc1 could also act to maintain open chromatin, as shown for Foxa1 in the liver (Reizel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Reizel et al., 2020.

claim: Both Foxc1 and Sox9 have expression in many tissues outside the skeletal system.
source: Given that both Foxc1 and Sox9 have expression in many tissues outside the skeletal system, it will also be important to determine whether additional factors help to further restrict their activity to chondrocyte enhancers within skeletogenic mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Additional factors may help to restrict Foxc1 and Sox9 activity to chondrocyte enhancers within skeletogenic mesenchyme.
source: Given that both Foxc1 and Sox9 have expression in many tissues outside the skeletal system, it will also be important to determine whether additional factors help to further restrict their activity to chondrocyte enhancers within skeletogenic mesenchyme.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: Chondrocytes were labeled by co-expression of sox10:Dsred and col2a1a:GFP transgenes at 72 hpf.
source: We labeled chondrocytes by co-expression of sox10:Dsred and col2a1a:GFP transgenes (Figure 1A) and isolated double-positive and control double-negative cells by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Double-positive and control double-negative cells were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).
source: We labeled chondrocytes by co-expression of sox10:Dsred and col2a1a:GFP transgenes (Figure 1A) and isolated double-positive and control double-negative cells by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the experimental method.

claim: A modified 'micro' version of ATAC-seq (µATACseq) was performed on sorted cells.
source: We then subjected these cells to a modified 'micro' version of the assay for transposase-accessible chromatin followed by next-generation sequencing (µATACseq).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the experimental method.

claim: Distal accessible elements were defined as regions excluding those within 1 kb upstream or 0.5 kb downstream of transcription start sites.
source: In order to focus on potential distal cis-regulatory elements, we excluded accessible regions within 1 kb upstream or 0.5 kb downstream of transcription start sites.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the analysis method.

claim: Nfat and Fox motifs were the second and third most co-enriched with Sox motifs in Sox9 ChIP-Seq of mouse chondrocytes.
source: Sox9 ChIP-Seq of mouse chondrocytes had previously revealed Nfat and Fox motifs as the second and third most co-enriched with Sox motifs (Ohba et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ohba et al., 2015.

claim: The Nkx motif might reflect the role of Nkx3.2 in cartilage differentiation.
source: and the Nkx motif might reflect the role of Nkx3.2 in cartilage differentiation (Provot et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Provot et al., 2006.

claim: The striking motif similarities between zebrafish and mouse indicate strong conservation of the cartilage gene regulatory network between fish and mammals.
source: These striking motif similarities indicate strong conservation of the cartilage gene regulatory network between fish and mammals, and between the face and rib
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of motifs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The striking motif similarities indicate strong conservation of the cartilage gene regulatory network between the face and rib.
source: These striking motif similarities indicate strong conservation of the cartilage gene regulatory network between fish and mammals, and between the face and rib
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of zebrafish facial chondrocytes and mouse rib chondrocytes.

claim: Many of the identified chondrocyte-specific accessible regions in zebrafish likely function as chondrocyte enhancers.
source: and strongly suggest that many of the identified chondrocyte-specific accessible regions in zebrafish likely function as chondrocyte enhancers.
evidence: This is an inference based on motif similarities and GO term enrichment.

claim: GO terms for neural crest cell migration and dorsal/ventral pattern formation likely reflect retention of enhancer accessibility linked to the neural crest origins and later dorsoventral arch patterning of the precursors of facial cartilage.
source: We also recovered terms for neural crest cell migration and dorsal/ventral pattern formation, likely reflecting retention of enhancer accessibility linked to the neural crest origins and later dorsoventral arch patterning of the precursors of facial cartilage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GO term results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Enrichment of Nkx motifs in Group II elements might reflect the role of Nkx3.2 in limiting chondrocyte maturation and promoting joint formation.
source: For example, enrichment of Nkx motifs in Group II elements might reflect the role of Nkx3.2 in limiting chondrocyte maturation (Provot et al., 2006) and promoting joint formation (Miller et al., 2003)
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Provot et al., 2006 and Miller et al., 2003.

claim: The preferential enrichment of the Tead motif in Group III elements might reflect the later proliferative expansion of chondrocytes.
source: while the preferential enrichment of the Tead motif, which is linked to growth-associated Hippo signaling (Ota and Sasaki, 2008), in Group III elements might reflect the later proliferative expansion of chondrocytes.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Ota and Sasaki, 2008.

claim: Cartilages of the upper/dorsal face fail to develop in zebrafish Foxc1 mutants.
source: In zebrafish Foxc1 (foxc1a−/−; foxc1b−/−) mutants, cartilages of the upper/dorsal face fail to develop (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2018.

claim: pou3f3b>GFP+; sox10:Dsred+ CNCCs were present at 48 hpf in Foxc1 mutants.
source: As pou3f3b>GFP+; sox10:Dsred+ CNCCs were present at 48 hpf (Figure 3A,B), we performed µATACseq on these cells after FACS from Foxc1 mutants and controls at 36 and 48 hpf.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3A,B.

claim: 79% of accessible regions in dorsal CNCCs and pan-CNCCs at 36 hpf had similar accessibility.
source: A comparison of the 15,781 accessible regions in dorsal CNCCs (pou3f3b>GFP+; sox10:Dsred+) and pan-CNCCs (fli1a:GFP+; sox10:Dsred+) at 36 hpf revealed 79% with similar accessibility, 11% with greater accessibility in dorsal CNCCs, and 10% with greater accessibility in pan-CNCCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 72% of accessible regions in dorsal CNCCs and pan-CNCCs at 48 hpf had similar accessibility.
source: Of 22,323 elements at 48 hpf, 72% were similarly accessible, 10% more accessible in dorsal CNCCs, and 18% more accessible in pan-CNCCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 96% of cartilage-specific elements displayed similar accessibility between dorsal- and pan-CNCCs at 36 hpf.
source: A comparison of the 5,736 regions with specific accessibility in cartilage at 72 hpf revealed high correlation between dorsal- and pan-CNCCs at 36 hpf, with 96% displaying similar accessibility (r = 0.92, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,C.

claim: 43% of cartilage-specific elements displayed greater accessibility in pan-CNCCs at 48 hpf.
source: By 48 hpf, however, we observed notable differences between accessibility of cartilage-specific elements, with 43% displaying greater accessibility in pan-CNCCs and only 0.2% displaying greater accessibility in dorsal CNCCs (r = 0.71, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,D.

claim: The decreased accessibility of cartilage-specific elements in dorsal CNCCs at 48 hpf supports that dorsal chondrocytes develop later than other chondrocytes in the zebrafish face.
source: The decreased accessibility of cartilage-specific elements in dorsal CNCCs at 48 hpf supports previous studies that dorsal chondrocytes develop later than other chondrocytes in the zebrafish face (Barske et al., 2016; Schilling and Kimmel, 1997).
evidence: This is an inference based on the accessibility data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Foxc1-dependent and Foxc1-independent cartilage elements may be commonly bound by Sox9 but likely differ in co-binding by Foxc1 and additional co-factors.
source: These findings suggest that Foxc1-dependent and -independent cartilage elements may be commonly bound by Sox9 but likely differ in co-binding by Foxc1 and additional co-factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the motif analysis showing Sox motifs in both groups but different Fox and other motifs.

claim: The presence of the Nkx motif only in Foxc1-independent elements suggests that it could be an alternative co-factor for Sox9.
source: For example, the presence of the Nkx motif only in Foxc1-independent elements suggests that it could be an alternative co-factor for Sox9, in line with the known roles for Nkx3.2 in chondrocyte biology (Provot et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculation based on motif analysis and supported by citation to Provot et al., 2006.

claim: 22 Foxc1-dependent Group II elements near 15 different genes were tested in zebrafish transgenic assays.
source: We tested 22 Foxc1-dependent Group II elements near 15 different genes, which included elements linked to genes with known cartilage function (ucmab, matn4, matn1, lect1, epyc, col9a1a, col9a3, sox10, acana, foxa3, mia) and others with unknown cartilage function (si:dkey33i1l.4, gas1b, lefty2, slc35d1a) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the experimental approach.

claim: Cartilage expression was confirmed in independent stable transgenic lines for all 13 positive elements.
source: We confirmed cartilage expression in independent stable transgenic lines for all 13 positive elements (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most cartilage enhancers drove expression in specific sub-regions or particular differentiation stages of cartilage.
source: Whereas an element in the first intron of sox10 drove uniform cartilage-specific expression, most elements drove expression in specific sub-regions or particular differentiation stages of cartilage.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the diverse expression patterns shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Testing of four Foxc1-independent Group II elements revealed two that drove cartilage expression.
source: Testing of four Foxc1-independent Group II elements revealed two that drove cartilage expression (distal 5′ elements of gas1b and matn4), one that drove cartilage, bone, and ligament expression (distal 5′ element of sparc), and one with no activity (promoter-associated element of sox10) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of tested Foxc1-dependent and -independent Group II elements are equally capable of driving cartilage expression.
source: Thus, the majority of tested Foxc1-dependent and -independent Group II elements are equally capable of driving cartilage expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transgenic assay results.

claim: Two tested Foxc1-independent Group I elements showed arch CNCC expression at 36 hpf and minimal cartilage expression at 6 dpf.
source: We also tested five Foxc1-independent Group I elements and found that two showed arch CNCC expression at 36 hpf and minimal cartilage expression at 6 dpf (prrx1a and emx3 elements), one no expression at 36 hpf and ligament expression at 6 dpf (satb2), and two no expression at either stage (prrx1a, cd248a) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: None of the 16 Group II elements that drove cartilage expression at 6 dpf showed 36 hpf arch CNCC expression.
source: In contrast, we did not observe 36 hpf arch CNCC expression in any of the 16 Group II elements that drove cartilage expression at 6 dpf.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the transgenic assay results.

claim: Most Group I elements tested likely represent either neural crest elements in the process of decommissioning or elements prefiguring non-cartilage fates.
source: As most of the Group I elements tested had decreased accessibility from 36 to 48 hpf, it seems likely that these elements represent either neural crest elements in the process of decommissioning (e.g. prrx1a and emx3) or elements prefiguring non-cartilage fates (e.g. satb2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the accessibility dynamics and expression patterns of Group I elements.

claim: Most cartilage enhancers appear to gain accessibility after 36 hpf.
source: Thus, most cartilage enhancers appear to gain accessibility after 36 hpf, with activity of late-opening cartilage enhancers in diverse locations, indicating that global cartilage expression patterns are achieved in part through the summation of enhancers with more restricted activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal accessibility analysis and transgenic assay results.

claim: Global cartilage expression patterns are achieved in part through the summation of enhancers with more restricted activity.
source: Thus, most cartilage enhancers appear to gain accessibility after 36 hpf, with activity of late-opening cartilage enhancers in diverse locations, indicating that global cartilage expression patterns are achieved in part through the summation of enhancers with more restricted activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the diverse spatial expression patterns of individual enhancers.
